meta.title: Who really said "In case you ever foolishly forget: I am never not thinking of you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Virginia Woolf. Woolf scholars find "foolishly forget" nowhere in her published works, letters or diaries. The Selected Diaries credit is wrong.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In case you ever foolishly forget: I am never not thinking of you'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely pinned on Virginia Woolf, but Woolf scholars find it in none of her works, letters or diaries. Its true source is still unknown.

answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — an untraced modern line
answer.sourceLine: Countless websites credit this line to Woolf, often to her Selected Diaries, but it appears nowhere in her published works. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ reports that “foolishly forget” does not occur in her writing, letters and diaries included. Scholars from both Woolf societies searched for it and are “stumped”.

source.excerpt: In case you ever foolishly forget: I am never not thinking of you
trail: 2015: a post on the “Virginia Woolf” Facebook page, which says it is run by “her publishers Everyman’s Library”, credits the line to Woolf with a Selected Diaries cover. The VWSGB calls this one of the earliest examples it found and notes that the addressee “you” makes a diary entry unlikely (VWSGB ↗).
Quote sites: Goodreads repeats the variant “Just in case you ever foolishly forget; I’m never not thinking of you” and says it is from Selected Diaries (Goodreads ↗).

January 2025: a query reaches the Woolf societies from someone who said she was working for Tiffany & Co and wanted permission to use the line in a campaign. On the VWoolf mailing list, Vara Neverow reports no hits in Google Books, Google Scholar or the Kindle Complete Works, where “Foolishly” appears only 18 times and never in this phrase. Another member found zero hits for “foolishly forget” in a Complete Works edition that includes the diaries (VWoolf list archive ↗).
Verdict: the VWSGB adds the line to its misquotations page and concludes that “foolishly forget” does not occur in Woolf’s published works, letters and diaries included: “we’re stumped!” (VWSGB ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the popular wording. A common variant reads “Just in case you ever foolishly forget; I’m never not thinking of you.” No original text exists to quote it in context: Woolf scholars have not found the line in anything she published.

source.rightsNote: No identifiable source exists, so no copyright status can be stated. The line is not in any of Woolf’s published works, and its anonymous author and first appearance are unknown. Quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for it.

author.heading: Virginia Woolf
author.metaLine: 1882–1941 · English modernist novelist, essayist, publisher & critic
author.bio: Virginia Woolf wrote Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927) and was a central figure of literary modernism. Her diaries and letters were published after her death, including her love letters to Vita Sackville-West. That makes her an easy target for romantic lines that sound like a letter but have no source.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Woolf
misattribution.intro: The line sounds like one of Woolf’s love letters to Vita Sackville-West. Online it travels with a specific-sounding citation, Selected Diaries, that does not hold up.

items.why: The 2015 Everyman’s Library Facebook post and Goodreads both credit Selected Diaries. The VWSGB notes that the line’s addressee “you” makes a diary entry unlikely, and that the phrase is not in her diaries or letters (VWSGB ↗).

items.who: Virginia Woolf, letters to Vita Sackville-West
items.why: The VWSGB says the line “might sound like part of a letter to Vita Sackville-West”, but “foolishly forget” does not occur in her published letters (VWSGB ↗).

items.who: Vita and Virginia (play or film), or a novel about Woolf
items.why: On the VWoolf list, Vara Neverow suggested the phrase was probably invented anonymously and might have come from the play or film Vita and Virginia or from a novel about Woolf. That was only a guess, and nobody has confirmed it (VWoolf list archive ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has found who wrote it. It does not come from Virginia Woolf’s published works, diaries or letters, according to the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: This misquote nearly went commercial. In January 2025 the Woolf societies were asked about permission to use the line in a Tiffany & Co campaign. That started a search across Woolf’s complete works, and it found nothing (VWoolf list archive ↗).

The case shows how a precise-looking citation can carry a fake quote. One early version came from a Facebook page that says it is run by Woolf’s own publisher, and it named a real book, Selected Diaries. The book is real. The line is not in it.
context.pull: Many people have tried to find the source … but we’re stumped!
